title: Topological mechanical metamaterial for robust and ductile one-way fracturing

paper_content.abstract: Fracturing is unavoidable and threatens the reliability and functionality of materials. Therefore, regulating the propagation of cracks in a predictable and ductile manner is of paramount importance. Herein, we exploit the properties of topological mechanical metamaterials (TMMs) as a versatile mechanism to guide cracks unidirectionally and turn fracturing of lattices made of brittle materials into ductile events. Inspired by quantum topological states, recent discoveries of TMMs have uncovered varieties of unconventional mechanical phenomena, ranging from one-way wave propagation to polar elasticity. We show that polarized floppy modes occurring in TMMs lead to strongly asymmetric stress fields localizing around the notch tips, leading to ductile one-way fracturing, in sharp contrast to classical theories of fractures in brittle materials. Our work demonstrates the universality of this fracture unidirectionality feature, which is protected by TMM’s bulk topology, and provides robust solutions in programmable fracturing for a broad class of materials and structures.
paper_content.introduction:
Fracture undermines the stability of structural and material systems across scales and physical realms, from rocks1, bones and teeth2,3, polymers4–12, to two-dimensional materials13–15 and microscalemolecules and fibers16–19. Fractures are inevitable; what one can do is design materials endowed with the ability to retard the manifestation of fracturing (crack initiation and propagation) or mitigate the severity of fracturing events to avoid the onset of catastrophic damage. To this end, understanding and subsequently controlling the parameters that guide fracture propagation remains a key challenge in theoretical and practical research in fracture mechanics20–32. Recently proposed methods to steer cracking direction include applying different external loading conditions23,33–35, controlling material anisotropy (e.g., using bio-inspired nacre36 and seashell)37, programming the micro-structure geometry38–41 and introducing local curvature42,43. However, it is a universal phenomenon in fracturing that sharp geometries of the initial notch, small defects and system imperfections can act as stress concentrators, influencing both crack initiation and propagation44, interfering with the control of cracking directions, leading to indeterminacy as observed in ref. 39. Despite this abundance of approaches, a more robust principle using geometry to guide the direction of fractures that is insensitive to notch geometries and imperfections is still lacking.

In the past decade, principles from quantum topological states of matter have been widely utilized to design mechanical metamaterials featuring topologically protected properties, such as one-way edge states and polarized elasticity45–49. Among them, Maxwell lattices have attracted extensive interest due to the ability to topologically control stress and strain fields, offering programmable soft boundaries45,50–52, transformable responses53–55, programmable stress distribution56–59, and low-frequency edge waves60,61. Earlier studies of TMMs have focused on exploring topological floppy modes49–54,60,61 rather than controlling stress fields. A handful of papers studied fracturing control using TMMs but they either focused on the capability of using states of self-stress to concentrate stress, predominately in small strain regimes before fracturing57–59, or only notches on the side62,63.

In this paper, we show that topological mechanics of Maxwell lattices can be used to robustly guide fractures to propagate in a unidirectional way even during the nonlinear fracturing process, and we demonstrate this effect using theories, simulations and experiments. We show that the topological protection of TMMs endow them with unidirectional cracking that is robust against geometric details. We find that the topological polarization, which controls the spatial patterns of the stress fields and specifically the regions of stress focusing, is responsible for strong asymmetries in the stress fields that localize around cracks, causing the lattice to fracture along a deterministic and predictable direction. Remarkably, this property is preserved even when the fracture progresses into the nonlinear regime. Moreover, the sequential activation of topological zero modes resulting from the onset of crack make the fracture process ductile, although the material the lattice is made from is brittle. Such geometry-induced effective ductility drastically reduces the occurrence of catastrophic failures.

We provide rationales for our results in light of topologically protected zero modes (ZMs) in Maxwell TMMs, and compare our results with linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM)64–67. Specifically, we find that topological ZMs generate stress distributions that significantly differ from those predicted by LEFM in terms of both asymmetries and angular profiles near the crack tip, thus providing drivers for crack propagation that differ qualitatively by those observed in classical media as well as in nonpolarized lattices.

In summary, the properties of TMMs enables several advances in fracture mechanics and engineering: (1) using the combination of purely periodic geometry and isotropic constituent materials, the initial cracks are guided in a unidirectional and robust way even considering the nonlinear deformation at crack tips and material nonlinearity, for a wide range crack shapes; (2) protected by topology, the TMM is less sensitive to defects from fabrication and variances of notch shapes. (3) the TMM turns a sudden, brittle and unpredictable failure into a ductile and predictable one with early indicators; (4) the TMM enables on-demand control of crack tip stress conditions and achieves diffusive and concentrated fracturing in the same material; (5) based on topological kagome lattices, the TMM is light-weight.
paper_content.results:
Fracture of Maxwell lattice TMMs
In a homogeneous material, stress fields focus at the two tips of a crack symmetrically (Fig. 1A)69. As a result, in practical scenarios involving brittle materials (Supplementary Fig. 1), the propagation direction (to the left or to the right) that the crack eventually follows is highly sensitive to the material’s defects or imperfections and thus hard to predict or control. Moreover, the damage process is sudden and often without significant prior deformation (Supplementary Movie 1). The aim of crack-guiding functional materials35,38,39 is to break the symmetry of the geometry and guide the crack propagation in a unidirectional and predictable way.

A trivial approach to breaking this symmetry could be obtained by modulating material constants or disrupting mirror symmetry in micro-geometry. Such approaches suffer from material and strain dependence. Here, in contrast, we explore the architecture of polarized Maxwell lattice-based TMMs (Fig. 1B) as a means to manipulate the stress field and direct the crack propagation in a robust way based on topological protection. Maxwell lattices are mechanical lattices with an equal number of degrees of freedom and constraints in the bulk, thus operating on the verge of mechanical instability. They are known to exhibit topologically polarized elasticity, which manifests as the localization of states of self stress (SSS) and zero modes (ZMs) at opposite edges of a finite lattice domain45,50–52.

Topologically polarized elasticity predicts that, by replacing a solid continuum (Fig. 1A) with a TMM (Fig. 1B), an asymmetric stress field emerges in the neighborhood of a notch. Note that, in a lattice, a notch effectively consists of a sequence of severed ligaments (serving as structural hinges) along a line. This scenario is depicted in Fig. 1B via FEM simulations and experimental data70. For the experiment, we cut a Polyethylenimine (PEI) film into the TMM geometry in Fig. 1B and sandwich it between a pair of polarizers (see “Methods”, Supplementary Fig. 2). After subjecting it to slight stretching, it reveals an asymmetric stress field, indicated by the colormap.

We compare (1) a continuum medium (Fig. 1A) with a slim notch, (2) a topological kagome lattice TMM (Fig. 1B) and (3) a regular kagome lattice (Fig. 2A) - the latter two cases featuring a line of severed hinges acting as crack. Applying the same amount of total stress to all configurations, we extract stress profiles along horizontal paths between the immediate neighborhood of the notch tips and the free boundaries (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4). For the two lattice configurations, we adopt the average von Mises stress in the structural hinges as a stress indicator (Methods). Among the three, only the topological kagome shows a strongly asymmetric stress field above the notch. (1) For the continuum medium, the stress decays as 1/\sqrt{r}, where r is the distance from the notch tip (gray curve in Fig. 1C), consistent with classical theories64–67. (2) For the TMM (green curve), interestingly, the left side of the crack does not display a stress build-up at the effective notch tip, while on the right side the tip stress is three times the bulk value. The fluctuations at the left edge are a signature of the floppy modes available on that open edge due to polarization. The deformation mode in the bulk is a combination of stretching and bending of the hinges. (3) For the regular kagome (orange curve), an increase of stress from the bulk to the crack tip is observed, albeit smoother than in the continuum medium and the right side of topological kagome (Supplementary Figs. 6, 7), which can be explained by the blunting effect of kagome lattices71,72. For this lattice, the dominant deformation mode in the bulk is stretching. In addition, the sudden drop of the stress near the free boundaries (Fig. 1C)71 can be explained by noting that, at a free boundary, due to the lack of constraints, the deformation mode switches locally to bending-dominated and exhibits the deepest boundary layer of the three cases.

We further show that the trend of asymmetric tip stresses in TMMs continues deep into the fracturing process, beyond the linear elastic states of stress considered in previous studies56–58, injecting asymmetry into the actual damage propagation regime. Large rotations at the notch tip demonstrate geometric nonlinearity (circles at the tip in Fig. 1I–K) and the failure process includes material nonlinearity. We test several samples for each medium type (continuum, regular kagome and TMM) featuring the same length, width, and notch size to extract some statistics of failure (Fig. 1D) and document the existence or lack thereof of crack propagation directionality in these systems. Specifically, we count the number of instances where the crack propagates left/right. As shown in Fig. 1D, when it comes to realistic experimental conditions, for the continuum medium and the regular kagome it is impossible to predict (or enforce) a priori which way the crack will propagate or induce symmetric, simultaneous, two-way propagation from both tips of the crack. This is despite the fact that they both show perfectly symmetric stress fields in simulations (Fig. 1C). In Fig. 1E, we report normalized experimental force-displacement curves acquired during the tests (Supplementary Fig. 6). The curve for the continuum samples (gray line) clearly shows a sharp drop from the peak state, representative of canonical brittle behavior. An intermediate and final cracked state of a continuum sample are shown in Fig. 1G and H, respectively. The paper sample undergoes infinitesimal deformation before undergoing sudden failure (Supplementary Movie 1), and the direction of crack propagation is unpredictable from one sample to the next.

In contrast, the TMM presents a much slower manifestation of failure reminiscent of ductile failure, as indicated by the green line in Fig. 1E, which features a jagged profile that stretches the failure process over an elongation range 5–6 times larger than that observed for the continuum (Supplementary Movie 2). Moreover, driven by the significant stress difference between the two tips (Fig. 1C), the crack propagates consistently to the right, as indicated by the 100% count in Fig. 1D. The local physical processes involved in crack opening for the TMM are documented in the snapshots of Fig. 1I-M. Interestingly, before cracking, the TMM gives a warning: in both simulations and experiments, the circled right tip hinge (brown circle) shows an opening angle larger than the others by ≈10° (Fig. 1I). The breaking of the first hinge on the right side corresponds to the first drop in the jagged force profile of Fig. 1E. At 203 s, with the first hinge broken, the largest stress is found in the second right tip hinge (circled), as shown in Fig. 1J. After that, the crack keeps propagating to the right, reaching the state of Fig. 1K at 333 s, with the second hinge broken and the largest stress found in the third hinge, and that of Fig. 1K at 600 s, when the one-way cracking pattern is fully formed in simulations. In the experiments, due to setup imperfections (e.g., hinge fabrication and mixed-mode loading, see Methods) and proximity to the free boundary, hinges on the left started to break earlier than expected. The final state shown in Fig. 1M at 1300 s mark the collapse point where the sample loses integrity. Inspection of the deformation and stress fields reveals something additional about the mechanics of the process. As the first hinge breaks and the second one carries the largest stress, it experiences a more pronounced bending deformation, which is accompanied by an increase in stiffness (Fig. 1E, I-L). When the second hinge goes to the maximum allowed strain and breaks, we observe stress concentration in the third hinge on the right at larger strain. This nonlinear phenomenon is due to the sequential activation of topological ZMs in the nonlinear regime, as we discuss in the next section.

Topological zero modes control the asymmetric stress field
The strongly asymmetric distribution of stress induced by crack opening in TMMs can be understood via the analysis of the localized topological ZMs45,48–51 that are triggered during the deformation process. Here we first discuss this effect in the case of ideal Maxwell lattices, featuring only nearest-neighbor (NN) bonds and then generalize it to structural TMMs featuring additional weak bending constraints which can be characterized by next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) bonds.

In the NN-only lattice, the nearly-ZMs near the notch leads to a strongly asymmetric displacement field. In a topological kagome lattice as an NN-bond only ideal Maxwell lattice, each node has two degrees of freedom from the in-plane displacements and two constraints from the four bonds connecting to it (as each bond is shared by 2 nodes). Maxwell’s counting rule of equal numbers of degrees of freedom and constraints is satisfied at every wavenumber, and the system has two homogeneous ZMs (x, y translations) and two homogeneous SSS that provide the elastic moduli for the coarse-grained lattice. Assume removing 1 node and 4 bonds in the bulk to open a small crack (Fig. 3A). This operation removes two degrees of freedom and four constraints, and as a result, it lifts the two homogeneous SSS (Supplementary Fig. 14A) and creates two nearly-ZMs near the notch (the even mode is shown in Fig. 3A). Different from ZMs, nearly-ZMs exhibit not exactly but nearly zero frequency. The frequencies of these two nearly-ZMs vanish exponentially as a function of the system size. A simulation of the ideal lattice (under either periodic boundary conditions or fixed boundary conditions, if the lattice is large) reveals the spatial pattern of these two nearly-ZMs, which are localized around the right tip of the notch, as a result of the topological polarization R_T, following the predictions of topological mechanics theories45,48,49. The two nearly-ZMs are even u(e) and odd u(o) with respect to the horizontal mirror plane of the notch, respectively, and they have dynamical frequencies λ_e, λ_o (corresponding to mode frequencies λ_e = m, λ_0 = m with m being the mass of the nodes). These two nearly-ZMs exhibit two supersymmetry partners, which are nearly-SSSs45, s(e) and s(o).

The response of the lattice upon an external load of y-stretching, as we derive in detail in the Supplementary Note IID, is dominated by the even nearly-ZM u(e) (Fig. 3A) via

u_i = u_i^{(aff)} + \sum_e \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_e}} s_e^{(b)} E_b^{(aff)} u_i^{(e)}, (1)

where i labels the nodes, b labels the bonds, u(aff), E(aff) are the affine (homogeneous strain) displacement and bond extension of the lattice under the load, and the nonaffine response is controlled by the even nearly-ZM u(e), with the coefficient given by the overlap of the affine strain E(aff) with the corresponding even nearly-SSS s(e).

A complimentary way to understand the topological nature of this strongly asymmetric displacement field is to realize that the bulk solution of ZMs in Maxwell lattices can be generally written in the form of e^{iq \cdot r}, where r is the position and the imaginary part of q controls the decay of the ZMs45,51,53. The horizontal topological polarization R_T of the lattices we consider here directly controls the imaginary part of q_x of the ZMs. For each given real q_y, there are two ZM solutions, both of which have the imaginary part q''_x > 0 for the topological kagome, but the two q''_x's have opposite signs for the twisted kagome which is unpolarized (Supplementary Fig. 11). The actual displacement field upon loading comes from a linear combination of these ZMs, with the coefficients determined by the boundary conditions. The notch in the middle allows for finite displacement amplitude around it. The displacement must decay towards the right in the topological kagome, consistent with the numerical results (Fig. 3). Importantly, if there is any displacement amplitude on the left tip, it must exponentially increase towards the bulk on the left, which is not allowed. This requires vanishing displacement on the left tip in the topological ideal Maxwell lattice case. In contrast, in the twisted kagome lattice, decay occurs in both ±x directions, giving a ratio of displacements of order unity between the two tips (Supplementary Fig. 11). This argument also generalizes this phenomenon from the one-node notch to other sizes and shapes of cut, as we mention below.

The discussions above describe the response of the NN-only topological Maxwell lattice under load, where due to the lack of SSSs48,49, the lattice moves along the linear combination of the affine strain and the nonaffine nearly-ZM (Eq. (1)), and there is no stress to the linear order (Supplementary Fig. 14A). The strong asymmetry of the nearly-ZM gives rise to the strong asymmetry of the displacement field of the lattice under load, leading to stress responses only at the nonlinear level (Supplementary Information IIE).

To fully understand the stress response of the TMM, we theoretically analyze the topological kagome lattice with NNN bonds, and compare with numerical results on the NNN lattice characterized by a spring constant ratio k_NNN/k_NN, and the TMM which is a continuum model characterized by normalized hinge thickness h/|a_1|. Firstly, we verify that despite the deviation from the ideal Maxwell limit, the displacement responses of the NNN lattice (Fig. 3B) and the TMM (Fig. 3C) under load is indeed dominated by the even nearly-ZM shown in Fig. 3A, featuring drastically different rotations at hinges at the left and right tips (Fig. 3D). Secondly, a subtle difference arises, as the weak additional constraints due to the NNN bonds or the bending stiffness of the hinges induce homogeneous SSS even in the presence of the notch. This leads to weak stress responses at the linear level, mainly carried by the NNN bonds (Fig. 3E). In contrast, the NN stress increases nonlinearly at small k_NNN/k_NN, as determined by the ideal theory which applies to marginally stable ideal lattices. When the NNN spring constant or the hinge thickness becomes large, the lattice deviates from the ideal Maxwell case and crosses over to normal elastic media behavior where geometric details prevail, with the topological polarization effect vanishing (Fig. 3F, G). This result further confirms that the observed asymmetric features originate primarily from topology rather than geometry. As the NNN spring constant increases, the lattice shape remains geometrically asymmetric, maintaining one sharp side and one blunt side, yet the stress difference between crack tips gradually diminishes (Fig. 3F). The tip stress difference can also be tuned by varying the unit cell geometry which controls the localization length of the topological ZMs, characterizing the polarization magnitude (Supplementary Note IIH). Less polarized configurations exhibit a weaker asymmetric feature. In practice, finding the best configuration is essential. Reducing the polarization, either by lowering its magnitude or by increasing the hinge thickness, weakens control over one-way cracking.

Due to the robustness of the topological polarization, this strong asymmetry of strain and stress applies more generally beyond this simple scenario of a small notch (Supplementary Fig. 12). When the notch is longer, more nearly-ZMs are generated. However, due to the topological nature of the ZM profiles in the bulk, the excited combination of ZM is still characterized by strong stress on the right, as shown in Fig. 1, Supplementary Information IIE and Supplementary Fig. 13. This also applies to notches of other shapes. For simplicity, we will just use the term “ZMs” to refer to both exact ZMs and nearly-ZMs in other sections.

Furthermore, as the first hinge on the right breaks due to high stress, the lattice gains more ZMs which again asymmetrically localize more on the right than on the left due to the topological polarization R_T. The process of nonlinear deformation along the ZMs, generating high bending stress which evolves into stretching stress at higher strain at the right tip, occurs again until the next hinge breaks, and repeats until all hinges on the right break, as we show in Fig. 1. The nonlinear excitation of the topological ZMs is behind the ductility of this fracturing process, although the original material is brittle.

Comparison with linear elastic fracture mechanics
It is instructive to compare the asymmetric stress fields observed in TMMs to the classical solution of linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM). In LEFM, the tip stress is symmetric between left and right tips, and the dependence of the tip stress field upon the angle around, and distance from, the crack tip can be treated as separated variables64–67. Our tests and simulations suggest that the stress fields established in the Maxwell TMMs fundamentally differ from the LEFM cases in both respects. To quantitatively study this effect, we compare four cases: a topologically polarized kagome TMM, a regular kagome lattice, an elastic continuum, and the analytical solution from LEFM. For TMM and regular kagome, the stress fields are shown in Fig. 4A and B, respectively. Since most stress localizes at the hinges, here, for visualization purposes, we extract the hinge stresses (see Material and Methods) and interpolate them over the entire sample domain to obtain a continuous effective stress field. The deviations from LEFM predictions can be agilely appreciated by inspection. The left-right symmetry is broken at the center of the tip, and this behavior is observed robustly for different values of the hinge thickness parameter h, as shown in Fig. 4E. Moreover, the angular stress dependence (profiles of stress vs. angle γ or γ) is different when sampled at different distances (radii) from the tip, as shown in Fig. 4C, violating the independence of the radial and angular variables in LEFM. Figure 4C also shows that the left and right tip stress fields feature qualitatively different angular dependence, revealing an additional element of asymmetry due to polarization. For completeness, an analogous study is given for the regular kagome (green curve) and for the continuum (dark gray curve with markers for numerical simulations and light gray curve for analytical solution) in Fig. 4D. Here, all the curves apply to all radii, as the dependence upon γ or γ is decoupled from that upon distance.

We further study the case of elliptical notches in a continuum, for which finite LEFM analytical solutions are available, with emphasis on the dependence on the crack aspect ratio a/b. In Fig. 4F we show the stress field for a reference choice of a/b in a continuum. Not surprisingly, the stress field is symmetric close and far from the notch. From LEFM, the stress magnitude varies with a/b as σ_tip = σ_∞(1 + 2a/b), where σ_∞ is the far-field stress64–67. In Fig. 4G, we fix b and only vary a, de facto sweeping the aspect ratio between 1 and 4 and we monitor the ratio between the stress in the bulk, where the stress plateaus and can be taken as the far-field stress, and the tip stress. The trend of the gray curves confirm the expected decay. The slight deviation between simulation (dark gray with markers) and analytical solution (light gray) is due to numerics and progressively vanishes upon mesh refinement.

In Fig. 4G we also repeat the analysis for the two considered lattices (TMM and regular kagome). Interestingly, here the tip-to-bulk stress ratio appears to be independent of a/b, with the usual asymmetry between left and right tip exhibited by the TMM. The independence on defect length implies special mechanical features of the TMM: compared to normal media, the metamaterial shows a larger fracture toughness with delayed cracking due to slower increase of stress focusing as notch size increases.

Topology-controlled fracture: a portfolio of patterns
The one-way fracture mechanism discussed above is not limited to straight line notches located in the bulk. It also applies to initial notches of different shapes or differently located in the lattice domain. This robustness attribute proceed directly to the fact that the ZM-controlled fracture mechanism is topologically protected. The importance of notch-shape insensitivity lies in the fact that naturally occurring notches in materials take on diverse forms due to various types of damage. Achieving a metamaterial that guides cracks unidirectionally regardless of notch shape would greatly expand the applicability of fracture control in complex environments.

We demonstrate this through three representative cases (schematically depicted and color-coded in Fig. 5A): (I) a tilted cut in the bulk (green), (II) a cut at the soft edge (blue), and (III) a cut at the rigid edge (orange). For (I), we first check the distribution of ZMs predicted by theory for the idealized NN lattice under periodic boundary conditions (similar to Fig. 3A). After removing sites and bonds along the direction of lattice vector a_2 (Fig. 1B, Methods), all the ZMs are localized asymmetrically at only the right edge of the crack in Fig. 5D, as a result of topological polarization. We then examine the problem for the corresponding TMM in Fig. 5E. Simulations indicate that, under uniform stretching of the lattice, the deformation localizes at the right edge as well (see displacement colormap in Fig. 5E). Consequently, the stress developed in the hinges on the right edge is greater than that at the left edge, as depicted in Fig. 5B (left). A similar asymmetric pattern of ZMs and stress localization can also be found for other crack shapes (e.g., the triangular hole in Supplementary Fig. 19).

To quantify this asymmetry, we define n as the vector normal to the notch edge and α the angle between n and the polarization vector R_T. It is known from theory of polarized Maxwell lattices that the density of ZMs at an edge is proportional to n · R_T = cos α45. As described below, we find this quantity to be a good indicator of stress distribution around holes. In Fig. 5F, we consider holes of different orientations and plot the magnitude of ZMs at the edge and the bulk-to-edge stress ratio against the angle α. When α approaches π (or cos α → -1), the edge has no localized ZMs (the left side of the crack in Fig. 3A, Fig. 5D) and shows the same hinge stress as the bulk stress (Fig. 4A). On the other hand, as α goes to 0, the stress ratio approaches 0, implying a significant stress concentration at the edge. Here, the hinge thickness is set to h/|a_1| = 0.015 in Fig. 5B, C, F.

This asymmetry of stress distribution leads to robustly controllable crack propagation directions for a variety of hole orientations occurring in TMM domains, which we demonstrate numerically and experimentally in Fig. 5G, H. The initial state has a notch along a_2 in Fig. 5G. After being stretched, both nonlinear simulations and experiments show that the crack initially propagates to the right, emanating from the bottom-right tip and breaking sequentially the two adjacent hinges (Fig. 3G). After that, the crack also propagates to the left side, as shown in the Supplementary Movie 8, likely due to the proximity of the crack to the right boundary. The results emphasize that the unidirectional cracking mechanism is invariant to the shape of the bulk notch (see one-way cracking of a triangle notch in Supplementary Movie 9 and a rectangular notch in Supplementary Movie 10).

The same principle also controls stress fields and crack propagation driven by edge cuts, with some noteworthy differences between soft (cases II) and rigid (cases III) edges. In Fig. 5C, via simulations we calculate and plot the stress developed along the hinges in the same row along which the crack propagates, from the notch tip to the other side of the sample. We observe qualitatively different trends between the two cases. When the initial notch is at the soft edge, the stress drops sharply into the bulk, whereas when the initial notch is at the rigid edge, the stress decreases gradually. Overall, the decay of the soft edge curve follows a trend similar to the decay of hinge stress along the right tip path observed for the bulk crack in Fig. 4C. As shown in the experiment with initial notch at the soft edge (Fig. 5I–J), since the tip hinge has a much larger stress than the surrounding hinges (Fig. 5B, middle), the crack always propagates along the straight path (Fig. 5J). In contrast, the stress at the rigid edge is diffusive, uniformly distributed around the tip, as indicated by the color of the dots in the K inset (consistent with the numerical prediction in Fig. 5C). This results in multiple potential crack paths, as observed in the experiments documented in Fig. 5K–M. As a result, small random perturbations caused by experimental non-idealities can cause unexpected bifurcations of the cracking paths. In Fig. 5L, the crack turns directly into the direction along a_2. In the cases shown Fig. 5M, the crack propagates straightly first and then turns into the direction along a_2 at a later stage. Furthermore, in both simulations and experiments, the rigid edge exhibits delayed cracking compared to the soft edge (Supplementary Fig. 22E, F), despite similar force peaks in the force-displacement curves for cases (II) and (III).

These differences in fracturing behavior between the two edges suggest that crack tips in TMM display a variety of regimes, ranging from stable propagation at the soft tip to diffusive cracking at the rigid tip. Diffusive failures, characterized by fracturing without stress concentration, typically occur in systems with high disorder or low connectivity24,25,73. Previously, people achieve concentrated stress and diffusive stress tips in different systems by tuning network connectivity74 or rigidity9,24,25. The former appears in highly connected or rigid systems, while the latter shows up in systems with low connectivity. Here, we demonstrate that both concentrated and diffusive stress can emerge within the same over-constrained real system, allowing for on-demand fracturing control.

Programming fracture sequences and fracture resistance
Topologically controlled fracturing sequences can also be further programmed to control fracture resistance and mechanical stiffness in more versatile ways. By incorporating more polarization directions in the lattice, we can generate distinct cracking paths that result in tunable fracture resistance (Fig. 6). Here, we compare the single-domain TMM (with one polarization direction; see Fig. 1) to interface-TMMs (featuring two opposed polarization directions, Fig. 6A, C). In these systems, the programmed interfaces play a dominant role over the notch tips, due to the excited SSSs in the interfaces. In the photoelastic experiments, concentrated stress is clearly observed at the interfaces for both geometries (Fig. 6B, D), and this finding is consistent with the simulations. In Fig. 6E, F, cracks first originate in the interface regions (the gray box). Once the interface hinges fail, especially those in the zigzag interface near the notch and all hinges in the straight interface, the crack extends toward the notches. Owing to the topological polarization effect, the crack propagates to the right tip before reaching the left tip.

Furthermore, the shape of the interfaces influences not only the cracking path but also the force-displacement curves and fracture resistance (Fig. 6H). In the straight interface configuration, all interface units experience highly concentrated stress and break almost simultaneously (Fig. 6D, F–H), resulting in the earliest cracking and the most brittle behavior among the configurations. In contrast, the tortuous path in the zigzag interface geometry creates stress gradients, causing the interface units to break sequentially in a more gradual manner rather than all at once. As a result, the zigzag interface configuration absorbs more energy and exhibits the highest fracture toughness and linear elastic stiffness (Fig. 6H inset). These results highlight how topological features can be leveraged to precisely program stress distributions, crack sequences, and fracture resistance.
paper_content.methods:
Experiments
We utilize Silhouette Cameo 4 Cutting Machine for cutting all the experiment samples. Our blade is the 0.2 mm Kraft Blade. We ensure that none of the hinges are broken before loading, to minimize initial imperfections. For the photoelastic setup in Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 2, we set one polarizer in the front of the sample and the other behind the sample (with a 90 deg angle difference of the transmitting axis of the front one). The photo elastic thin film is PEI film with a thickness of 0.076 mm, purchased from McMASTER-CARR. The loading is performed quasi-statically, with a speed of 2 mm per minute. In Fig. 1, sample width w = 152.4 mm, sample length L = 157 mm, crack length 2a = 75 mm, and hinge thickness h ≈ 0.8 mm (h/|a_1| = 0.06) in Fig. 1H-L and Fig. 5G, H, I-M. Compared to idealized simulations, out-of-plane deformation in experimental tests of thin lattices can slow the rapid force drop and delays the cracking process77.

In Figs. 1 (D-M) and 5, the cardboard paper is the Wexford Folder 2-pocket (0.26 mm thick), purchased from Walgreens. Each paper sample weighs 3.6 g. The loading machine is Instron 4301 equipped with a 100 N loading cell and a 10 kN load cell. To allow uniform stretching/clamping at the top/bottom boundaries, we prepare four aluminum pieces (1.6 mm thick), sandwich each of the two sides between two pieces and glue them together. In Fig. 1D, for each of the three geometries, ten samples are loaded to observe the probabilities of fracturing direction.

In Fig. 2, we quantitatively characterize the triangular lattice, the regular kagome lattice, the twisted kagome lattice and the TMM. The ductility is measured as the elongation ratio at failure, Δ_c/l_0, where Δ_c is the critical displacement at the force peak and l_0 is the original sample length44. The fracture toughness is calculated as the critical stress intensity factor σ_c \sqrt{\pi a f(a/W)}, where σ_c is the critical stress applied, 2a is the full crack length, and f(a/W) is a specimen geometry dependent function of the crack length a and sample width W44. The consumed energy is ∫F dx, where F is the applied force and x is the displacement44. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 10H, fabricated hinge thickness shows a measure average 0.8 ± 0.2 mm. We measured 20% of the hinges in 10 representative samples (≈400 hinges in total). reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors investigated the fracture behaviors of topological mechanical metamaterials (TMMs) and compared their behavior with that of continuum material and regular Kagome lattices. They demonstrated the directional asymmetry in the fracture behavior of TMMs, which contrasts with the symmetry behaviors of continuum materials and regular Kagome lattices. Overall, the novelty of the current study is limited, as the authors primarily examined the fracture behaviors of an existing structure TMM, which has already been extensively studied (e.g., refs. [48-52]) including its fracture properties (ref. [56]). Furthermore, the current study lacks the depth, as it merely presents qualitative phenomena without providing a quantitative comparison of fracture toughness. The reported phenomena of directional asymmetry in fracture behavior are also not novel (PRL, 126, 025503, 2021). Furthermore, some claims appear to be overstated (see comment #4 below). Therefore, the current manuscript cannot be recommended for publication in Nature Communications. Specific comments are given below:
1. The novelty of the study is limited. There are many existing studies on TMMs, including those from the same authors (refs. [48-52, 56-60]). Regarding fracture properties, it is not surprising that such an asymmetric structure exhibits directional asymmetry in fracture behavior, as in one direction the crack tip is sharp and the structure is weaker while in the other direction the crack tip is blunt and the structure is stronger. The concept of “fracture unidirectionality feature” is not new either (ref. [39] PRL, 126, 025503, 2021). The current study simply demonstrates the directional asymmetry in fracture behavior for an existing structure without providing new insights into how such designs could achieve superior fracture resistance.
2. The current study does not provide any quantitative comparison beyond showing the phenomena. For example, in Fig. 1E and Fig. S6, only the normalized force (force/peak force) is reported. The authors are suggested to provide the absolute force-displacement curves and calculate the fracture toughness of TMMs, and compare these results with those of regular Kagome lattices and other benchmark lattices, such as triangular lattices. Because it would be better to confirm whether TMMs achieve such fracture properties at significant expense of load-bearing capacity.
3. Even though using the normalized force, it seems that the regular Kagome lattices experimentally outperforms the TMMs in terms of fracture resistance (Fig. S6C). Furthermore, the discrepancy between simulations and experiments should be addressed.
4. In the Introduction Line 26, the claim of “Despite this abundance of approaches, a robust general principle for using geometry to guide the direction of fractures is still lacking.” seems overstated. The current study does not seem to provide a robust general principle either. In Line 50, it is stated that “the TMM is light-weighted and features material-invariant and scale-invariant properties.” Although it may be true for “material-invariant and scale-invariant”, there are no results in the manuscript that directly support this.
5. In Fig. 4, it is seen that the upper gripper rotated during loading. The authors are suggested to improve the mechanical testing setup to ensure uniaxial loading and provide the loading-displacement curves to make the results more quantitative. Moreover, the demonstration in Fig. 4 is too simple. It would be better to show how to engineer a tortuous crack path that leads to superior toughness through such asymmetry design.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The paper by Wang et al. uses topological metamaterials to control fracture. In particular, since topological metamaterials are polarized---they host asymmetric floppy modes, the fracture propagation becomes unidirectional and leads to large deformations before failure. As a consequence, the metamaterial appears ductile even though it is made from a brittle material.
As clearly described in the manuscript, the mechanism at stake is stress asymmetry, that comes from the topological polarization, the distorted Kagome unit cells are floppy on one side, therefore tend to deform without stretching any of the bonds on this side. In contrast, the opposite size exhibits no such zero energy deformation and the bonds tend to stretch when load is applied. What the authors show is that this simplified picture of the balls-and-springs holds even when the metamaterial is made from a continuous material rather than discrete springs, i.e. when the geometry is made from real hinges. Whereas the floppy hinges exhibit low stress, the opposite hinges undergo high stresses and hence break first. This is the reason why the fractures tends to propagate in one direction and, as the authors show, even turn around when the notch is created on the side with high stresses.
The main take away from this work is that topological metamaterials offer a new paradigm to control fracture, in a way that is very different from classical fracture mechanics. Fracture metamaterials have recently emerged as a promising area of research, but so far broadly applicable design concepts are missing. The present work establishes topology as a promising approach and hold the potential to become a seminal work. Therefore I think this paper is potentially an excellent fit for Nature Communications. I however think that the control of fracture displayed in the manuscript in its present form remains rather limited. The key attribute of metamaterials is their tunability. I think that the manuscript would reach a much higher impact if the authors were able to provide more compelling demonstrations of fracture control by utilizing further the design freedom at their disposal and topological floppy modes as a guide. Besides this main concern (which I believe the authors are well equipped to address), I list below some comments, which might help the authors further improve their manuscript.
*1 The authors argue that the unidirectionality of the fracture is protected by topology and is therefore less sensitive to defects and imperfection. It would perhaps be worth to back up that statement, especially since fracture is a phenomenon that is known to be extremely sensitive to imperfections. In particular, to which extend is the approach more robust that the asymmetric fracture reported in ref [39]?
*2 Is topology really essential here? What happens if one take a twisted (undistorted) Kagome instead? Would such metamaterial exhibit symmetric fracture instead?
*3 Likewise, does the magnitude of the topological polarization matter for unidirectional facture propagation? I would expect a topological metamaterials with a small polarization/asymmetry to be less robust to imperfections?
*4 Section 2.2 can be understood by physicists well versed in topological metamaterials but less so by scientists with no background in this area. The authors might want to make that section a bit more pedagogical to extend the reach of their paper.
*5 The authors often refer to supplementary figures from the Main Text, which make the read somewhat cumbersome and gives the impression that key information is given in the SI rather than in the Main Text. For instance, the comparison with continuous media in Fig. 1 is somewhat of a naive benchmark. From the text it seems that comparing with the undistorted Kagome would be more meaningful (and would allow less back and forth between Main Text and Supplementary Information).
*6 Topological metamaterials can host states of self-stress. What is the role of those states of self stress on the fracture propagation?
*7 Higher order topological metamaterials can host corner modes, would such corner modes be beneficial for the control of fracture?
*8 More generally, to reflect my main concern above, it would be important to know what the range of control one can achieve with topological metamaterials as well at the limitations.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Fracturing is unavoidable and threatens the reliability and functionality of materials. Therefore, regulating the propagation of cracks in a predictable and ductile manner is of paramount importance. Herein, we exploit the properties of topological mechanical metamaterials (TMMs) as a versatile mechanism to guide cracks unidirectionally and turn fracturing of lattices made of brittle materials into ductile events. Inspired by quantum topological states, recent discoveries of TMMs have uncovered varieties of unconventional mechanical phenomena, ranging from one-way wave propagation to polar elasticity. We show that polarized floppy modes occurring in TMMs lead to strongly asymmetric stress fields localizing around the notch tips, leading to ductile one-way fracturing, in sharp contrast to classical theories of fractures in brittle materials. Our work demonstrates the universality of this fracture unidirectionality feature, which is protected by TMM’s bulk topology, and provides robust solutions in programmable fracturing for a broad class of materials and structures.

---

## Introduction

Fracture undermines the stability of structural and material systems across scales and physical realms, from rocks1, bones and teeth2,3, polymers4–12, to two-dimensional materials13–15 and microscalemolecules and fibers16–19. Fractures are inevitable; what one can do is design materials endowed with the ability to retard the manifestation of fracturing (crack initiation and propagation) or mitigate the severity of fracturing events to avoid the onset of catastrophic damage. To this end, understanding and subsequently controlling the parameters that guide fracture propagation remains a key challenge in theoretical and practical research in fracture mechanics20–32. Recently proposed methods to steer cracking direction include applying different external loading conditions23,33–35, controlling material anisotropy (e.g., using bio-inspired nacre36 and seashell)37, programming the micro-structure geometry38–41 and introducing local curvature42,43. However, it is a universal phenomenon in fracturing that sharp geometries of the initial notch, small defects and system imperfections can act as stress concentrators, influencing both crack initiation and propagation44, interfering with the control of cracking directions, leading to indeterminacy as observed in ref. 39. Despite this abundance of approaches, a more robust principle using geometry to guide the direction of fractures that is insensitive to notch geometries and imperfections is still lacking.

In the past decade, principles from quantum topological states of matter have been widely utilized to design mechanical metamaterials featuring topologically protected properties, such as one-way edge states and polarized elasticity45–49. Among them, Maxwell lattices have attracted extensive interest due to the ability to topologically control stress and strain fields, offering programmable soft boundaries45,50–52, transformable responses53–55, programmable stress distribution56–59, and low-frequency edge waves60,61. Earlier studies of TMMs have focused on exploring topological floppy modes49–54,60,61 rather than controlling stress fields. A handful of papers studied fracturing control using TMMs but they either focused on the capability of using states of self-stress to concentrate stress, predominately in small strain regimes before fracturing57–59, or only notches on the side62,63.

In this paper, we show that topological mechanics of Maxwell lattices can be used to robustly guide fractures to propagate in a unidirectional way even during the nonlinear fracturing process, and we demonstrate this effect using theories, simulations and experiments. We show that the topological protection of TMMs endow them with unidirectional cracking that is robust against geometric details. We find that the topological polarization, which controls the spatial patterns of the stress fields and specifically the regions of stress focusing, is responsible for strong asymmetries in the stress fields that localize around cracks, causing the lattice to fracture along a deterministic and predictable direction. Remarkably, this property is preserved even when the fracture progresses into the nonlinear regime. Moreover, the sequential activation of topological zero modes resulting from the onset of crack make the fracture process ductile, although the material the lattice is made from is brittle. Such geometry-induced effective ductility drastically reduces the occurrence of catastrophic failures.

We provide rationales for our results in light of topologically protected zero modes (ZMs) in Maxwell TMMs, and compare our results with linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM)64–67. Specifically, we find that topological ZMs generate stress distributions that significantly differ from those predicted by LEFM in terms of both asymmetries and angular profiles near the crack tip, thus providing drivers for crack propagation that differ qualitatively by those observed in classical media as well as in nonpolarized lattices.

In summary, the properties of TMMs enables several advances in fracture mechanics and engineering: (1) using the combination of purely periodic geometry and isotropic constituent materials, the initial cracks are guided in a unidirectional and robust way even considering the nonlinear deformation at crack tips and material nonlinearity, for a wide range crack shapes; (2) protected by topology, the TMM is less sensitive to defects from fabrication and variances of notch shapes. (3) the TMM turns a sudden, brittle and unpredictable failure into a ductile and predictable one with early indicators; (4) the TMM enables on-demand control of crack tip stress conditions and achieves diffusive and concentrated fracturing in the same material; (5) based on topological kagome lattices, the TMM is light-weight.

---

## Results

Fracture of Maxwell lattice TMMs
In a homogeneous material, stress fields focus at the two tips of a crack symmetrically (Fig. 1A)69. As a result, in practical scenarios involving brittle materials (Supplementary Fig. 1), the propagation direction (to the left or to the right) that the crack eventually follows is highly sensitive to the material’s defects or imperfections and thus hard to predict or control. Moreover, the damage process is sudden and often without significant prior deformation (Supplementary Movie 1). The aim of crack-guiding functional materials35,38,39 is to break the symmetry of the geometry and guide the crack propagation in a unidirectional and predictable way.

A trivial approach to breaking this symmetry could be obtained by modulating material constants or disrupting mirror symmetry in micro-geometry. Such approaches suffer from material and strain dependence. Here, in contrast, we explore the architecture of polarized Maxwell lattice-based TMMs (Fig. 1B) as a means to manipulate the stress field and direct the crack propagation in a robust way based on topological protection. Maxwell lattices are mechanical lattices with an equal number of degrees of freedom and constraints in the bulk, thus operating on the verge of mechanical instability. They are known to exhibit topologically polarized elasticity, which manifests as the localization of states of self stress (SSS) and zero modes (ZMs) at opposite edges of a finite lattice domain45,50–52.

Topologically polarized elasticity predicts that, by replacing a solid continuum (Fig. 1A) with a TMM (Fig. 1B), an asymmetric stress field emerges in the neighborhood of a notch. Note that, in a lattice, a notch effectively consists of a sequence of severed ligaments (serving as structural hinges) along a line. This scenario is depicted in Fig. 1B via FEM simulations and experimental data70. For the experiment, we cut a Polyethylenimine (PEI) film into the TMM geometry in Fig. 1B and sandwich it between a pair of polarizers (see “Methods”, Supplementary Fig. 2). After subjecting it to slight stretching, it reveals an asymmetric stress field, indicated by the colormap.

We compare (1) a continuum medium (Fig. 1A) with a slim notch, (2) a topological kagome lattice TMM (Fig. 1B) and (3) a regular kagome lattice (Fig. 2A) - the latter two cases featuring a line of severed hinges acting as crack. Applying the same amount of total stress to all configurations, we extract stress profiles along horizontal paths between the immediate neighborhood of the notch tips and the free boundaries (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4). For the two lattice configurations, we adopt the average von Mises stress in the structural hinges as a stress indicator (Methods). Among the three, only the topological kagome shows a strongly asymmetric stress field above the notch. (1) For the continuum medium, the stress decays as 1/\sqrt{r}, where r is the distance from the notch tip (gray curve in Fig. 1C), consistent with classical theories64–67. (2) For the TMM (green curve), interestingly, the left side of the crack does not display a stress build-up at the effective notch tip, while on the right side the tip stress is three times the bulk value. The fluctuations at the left edge are a signature of the floppy modes available on that open edge due to polarization. The deformation mode in the bulk is a combination of stretching and bending of the hinges. (3) For the regular kagome (orange curve), an increase of stress from the bulk to the crack tip is observed, albeit smoother than in the continuum medium and the right side of topological kagome (Supplementary Figs. 6, 7), which can be explained by the blunting effect of kagome lattices71,72. For this lattice, the dominant deformation mode in the bulk is stretching. In addition, the sudden drop of the stress near the free boundaries (Fig. 1C)71 can be explained by noting that, at a free boundary, due to the lack of constraints, the deformation mode switches locally to bending-dominated and exhibits the deepest boundary layer of the three cases.

We further show that the trend of asymmetric tip stresses in TMMs continues deep into the fracturing process, beyond the linear elastic states of stress considered in previous studies56–58, injecting asymmetry into the actual damage propagation regime. Large rotations at the notch tip demonstrate geometric nonlinearity (circles at the tip in Fig. 1I–K) and the failure process includes material nonlinearity. We test several samples for each medium type (continuum, regular kagome and TMM) featuring the same length, width, and notch size to extract some statistics of failure (Fig. 1D) and document the existence or lack thereof of crack propagation directionality in these systems. Specifically, we count the number of instances where the crack propagates left/right. As shown in Fig. 1D, when it comes to realistic experimental conditions, for the continuum medium and the regular kagome it is impossible to predict (or enforce) a priori which way the crack will propagate or induce symmetric, simultaneous, two-way propagation from both tips of the crack. This is despite the fact that they both show perfectly symmetric stress fields in simulations (Fig. 1C). In Fig. 1E, we report normalized experimental force-displacement curves acquired during the tests (Supplementary Fig. 6). The curve for the continuum samples (gray line) clearly shows a sharp drop from the peak state, representative of canonical brittle behavior. An intermediate and final cracked state of a continuum sample are shown in Fig. 1G and H, respectively. The paper sample undergoes infinitesimal deformation before undergoing sudden failure (Supplementary Movie 1), and the direction of crack propagation is unpredictable from one sample to the next.

In contrast, the TMM presents a much slower manifestation of failure reminiscent of ductile failure, as indicated by the green line in Fig. 1E, which features a jagged profile that stretches the failure process over an elongation range 5–6 times larger than that observed for the continuum (Supplementary Movie 2). Moreover, driven by the significant stress difference between the two tips (Fig. 1C), the crack propagates consistently to the right, as indicated by the 100% count in Fig. 1D. The local physical processes involved in crack opening for the TMM are documented in the snapshots of Fig. 1I-M. Interestingly, before cracking, the TMM gives a warning: in both simulations and experiments, the circled right tip hinge (brown circle) shows an opening angle larger than the others by ≈10° (Fig. 1I). The breaking of the first hinge on the right side corresponds to the first drop in the jagged force profile of Fig. 1E. At 203 s, with the first hinge broken, the largest stress is found in the second right tip hinge (circled), as shown in Fig. 1J. After that, the crack keeps propagating to the right, reaching the state of Fig. 1K at 333 s, with the second hinge broken and the largest stress found in the third hinge, and that of Fig. 1K at 600 s, when the one-way cracking pattern is fully formed in simulations. In the experiments, due to setup imperfections (e.g., hinge fabrication and mixed-mode loading, see Methods) and proximity to the free boundary, hinges on the left started to break earlier than expected. The final state shown in Fig. 1M at 1300 s mark the collapse point where the sample loses integrity. Inspection of the deformation and stress fields reveals something additional about the mechanics of the process. As the first hinge breaks and the second one carries the largest stress, it experiences a more pronounced bending deformation, which is accompanied by an increase in stiffness (Fig. 1E, I-L). When the second hinge goes to the maximum allowed strain and breaks, we observe stress concentration in the third hinge on the right at larger strain. This nonlinear phenomenon is due to the sequential activation of topological ZMs in the nonlinear regime, as we discuss in the next section.

Topological zero modes control the asymmetric stress field
The strongly asymmetric distribution of stress induced by crack opening in TMMs can be understood via the analysis of the localized topological ZMs45,48–51 that are triggered during the deformation process. Here we first discuss this effect in the case of ideal Maxwell lattices, featuring only nearest-neighbor (NN) bonds and then generalize it to structural TMMs featuring additional weak bending constraints which can be characterized by next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) bonds.

In the NN-only lattice, the nearly-ZMs near the notch leads to a strongly asymmetric displacement field. In a topological kagome lattice as an NN-bond only ideal Maxwell lattice, each node has two degrees of freedom from the in-plane displacements and two constraints from the four bonds connecting to it (as each bond is shared by 2 nodes). Maxwell’s counting rule of equal numbers of degrees of freedom and constraints is satisfied at every wavenumber, and the system has two homogeneous ZMs (x, y translations) and two homogeneous SSS that provide the elastic moduli for the coarse-grained lattice. Assume removing 1 node and 4 bonds in the bulk to open a small crack (Fig. 3A). This operation removes two degrees of freedom and four constraints, and as a result, it lifts the two homogeneous SSS (Supplementary Fig. 14A) and creates two nearly-ZMs near the notch (the even mode is shown in Fig. 3A). Different from ZMs, nearly-ZMs exhibit not exactly but nearly zero frequency. The frequencies of these two nearly-ZMs vanish exponentially as a function of the system size. A simulation of the ideal lattice (under either periodic boundary conditions or fixed boundary conditions, if the lattice is large) reveals the spatial pattern of these two nearly-ZMs, which are localized around the right tip of the notch, as a result of the topological polarization R_T, following the predictions of topological mechanics theories45,48,49. The two nearly-ZMs are even u(e) and odd u(o) with respect to the horizontal mirror plane of the notch, respectively, and they have dynamical frequencies λ_e, λ_o (corresponding to mode frequencies λ_e = m, λ_0 = m with m being the mass of the nodes). These two nearly-ZMs exhibit two supersymmetry partners, which are nearly-SSSs45, s(e) and s(o).

The response of the lattice upon an external load of y-stretching, as we derive in detail in the Supplementary Note IID, is dominated by the even nearly-ZM u(e) (Fig. 3A) via

u_i = u_i^{(aff)} + \sum_e \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_e}} s_e^{(b)} E_b^{(aff)} u_i^{(e)}, (1)

where i labels the nodes, b labels the bonds, u(aff), E(aff) are the affine (homogeneous strain) displacement and bond extension of the lattice under the load, and the nonaffine response is controlled by the even nearly-ZM u(e), with the coefficient given by the overlap of the affine strain E(aff) with the corresponding even nearly-SSS s(e).

A complimentary way to understand the topological nature of this strongly asymmetric displacement field is to realize that the bulk solution of ZMs in Maxwell lattices can be generally written in the form of e^{iq \cdot r}, where r is the position and the imaginary part of q controls the decay of the ZMs45,51,53. The horizontal topological polarization R_T of the lattices we consider here directly controls the imaginary part of q_x of the ZMs. For each given real q_y, there are two ZM solutions, both of which have the imaginary part q''_x > 0 for the topological kagome, but the two q''_x's have opposite signs for the twisted kagome which is unpolarized (Supplementary Fig. 11). The actual displacement field upon loading comes from a linear combination of these ZMs, with the coefficients determined by the boundary conditions. The notch in the middle allows for finite displacement amplitude around it. The displacement must decay towards the right in the topological kagome, consistent with the numerical results (Fig. 3). Importantly, if there is any displacement amplitude on the left tip, it must exponentially increase towards the bulk on the left, which is not allowed. This requires vanishing displacement on the left tip in the topological ideal Maxwell lattice case. In contrast, in the twisted kagome lattice, decay occurs in both ±x directions, giving a ratio of displacements of order unity between the two tips (Supplementary Fig. 11). This argument also generalizes this phenomenon from the one-node notch to other sizes and shapes of cut, as we mention below.

The discussions above describe the response of the NN-only topological Maxwell lattice under load, where due to the lack of SSSs48,49, the lattice moves along the linear combination of the affine strain and the nonaffine nearly-ZM (Eq. (1)), and there is no stress to the linear order (Supplementary Fig. 14A). The strong asymmetry of the nearly-ZM gives rise to the strong asymmetry of the displacement field of the lattice under load, leading to stress responses only at the nonlinear level (Supplementary Information IIE).

To fully understand the stress response of the TMM, we theoretically analyze the topological kagome lattice with NNN bonds, and compare with numerical results on the NNN lattice characterized by a spring constant ratio k_NNN/k_NN, and the TMM which is a continuum model characterized by normalized hinge thickness h/|a_1|. Firstly, we verify that despite the deviation from the ideal Maxwell limit, the displacement responses of the NNN lattice (Fig. 3B) and the TMM (Fig. 3C) under load is indeed dominated by the even nearly-ZM shown in Fig. 3A, featuring drastically different rotations at hinges at the left and right tips (Fig. 3D). Secondly, a subtle difference arises, as the weak additional constraints due to the NNN bonds or the bending stiffness of the hinges induce homogeneous SSS even in the presence of the notch. This leads to weak stress responses at the linear level, mainly carried by the NNN bonds (Fig. 3E). In contrast, the NN stress increases nonlinearly at small k_NNN/k_NN, as determined by the ideal theory which applies to marginally stable ideal lattices. When the NNN spring constant or the hinge thickness becomes large, the lattice deviates from the ideal Maxwell case and crosses over to normal elastic media behavior where geometric details prevail, with the topological polarization effect vanishing (Fig. 3F, G). This result further confirms that the observed asymmetric features originate primarily from topology rather than geometry. As the NNN spring constant increases, the lattice shape remains geometrically asymmetric, maintaining one sharp side and one blunt side, yet the stress difference between crack tips gradually diminishes (Fig. 3F). The tip stress difference can also be tuned by varying the unit cell geometry which controls the localization length of the topological ZMs, characterizing the polarization magnitude (Supplementary Note IIH). Less polarized configurations exhibit a weaker asymmetric feature. In practice, finding the best configuration is essential. Reducing the polarization, either by lowering its magnitude or by increasing the hinge thickness, weakens control over one-way cracking.

Due to the robustness of the topological polarization, this strong asymmetry of strain and stress applies more generally beyond this simple scenario of a small notch (Supplementary Fig. 12). When the notch is longer, more nearly-ZMs are generated. However, due to the topological nature of the ZM profiles in the bulk, the excited combination of ZM is still characterized by strong stress on the right, as shown in Fig. 1, Supplementary Information IIE and Supplementary Fig. 13. This also applies to notches of other shapes. For simplicity, we will just use the term “ZMs” to refer to both exact ZMs and nearly-ZMs in other sections.

Furthermore, as the first hinge on the right breaks due to high stress, the lattice gains more ZMs which again asymmetrically localize more on the right than on the left due to the topological polarization R_T. The process of nonlinear deformation along the ZMs, generating high bending stress which evolves into stretching stress at higher strain at the right tip, occurs again until the next hinge breaks, and repeats until all hinges on the right break, as we show in Fig. 1. The nonlinear excitation of the topological ZMs is behind the ductility of this fracturing process, although the original material is brittle.

Comparison with linear elastic fracture mechanics
It is instructive to compare the asymmetric stress fields observed in TMMs to the classical solution of linear elastic fracture mechanics (LEFM). In LEFM, the tip stress is symmetric between left and right tips, and the dependence of the tip stress field upon the angle around, and distance from, the crack tip can be treated as separated variables64–67. Our tests and simulations suggest that the stress fields established in the Maxwell TMMs fundamentally differ from the LEFM cases in both respects. To quantitatively study this effect, we compare four cases: a topologically polarized kagome TMM, a regular kagome lattice, an elastic continuum, and the analytical solution from LEFM. For TMM and regular kagome, the stress fields are shown in Fig. 4A and B, respectively. Since most stress localizes at the hinges, here, for visualization purposes, we extract the hinge stresses (see Material and Methods) and interpolate them over the entire sample domain to obtain a continuous effective stress field. The deviations from LEFM predictions can be agilely appreciated by inspection. The left-right symmetry is broken at the center of the tip, and this behavior is observed robustly for different values of the hinge thickness parameter h, as shown in Fig. 4E. Moreover, the angular stress dependence (profiles of stress vs. angle γ or γ) is different when sampled at different distances (radii) from the tip, as shown in Fig. 4C, violating the independence of the radial and angular variables in LEFM. Figure 4C also shows that the left and right tip stress fields feature qualitatively different angular dependence, revealing an additional element of asymmetry due to polarization. For completeness, an analogous study is given for the regular kagome (green curve) and for the continuum (dark gray curve with markers for numerical simulations and light gray curve for analytical solution) in Fig. 4D. Here, all the curves apply to all radii, as the dependence upon γ or γ is decoupled from that upon distance.

We further study the case of elliptical notches in a continuum, for which finite LEFM analytical solutions are available, with emphasis on the dependence on the crack aspect ratio a/b. In Fig. 4F we show the stress field for a reference choice of a/b in a continuum. Not surprisingly, the stress field is symmetric close and far from the notch. From LEFM, the stress magnitude varies with a/b as σ_tip = σ_∞(1 + 2a/b), where σ_∞ is the far-field stress64–67. In Fig. 4G, we fix b and only vary a, de facto sweeping the aspect ratio between 1 and 4 and we monitor the ratio between the stress in the bulk, where the stress plateaus and can be taken as the far-field stress, and the tip stress. The trend of the gray curves confirm the expected decay. The slight deviation between simulation (dark gray with markers) and analytical solution (light gray) is due to numerics and progressively vanishes upon mesh refinement.

In Fig. 4G we also repeat the analysis for the two considered lattices (TMM and regular kagome). Interestingly, here the tip-to-bulk stress ratio appears to be independent of a/b, with the usual asymmetry between left and right tip exhibited by the TMM. The independence on defect length implies special mechanical features of the TMM: compared to normal media, the metamaterial shows a larger fracture toughness with delayed cracking due to slower increase of stress focusing as notch size increases.

Topology-controlled fracture: a portfolio of patterns
The one-way fracture mechanism discussed above is not limited to straight line notches located in the bulk. It also applies to initial notches of different shapes or differently located in the lattice domain. This robustness attribute proceed directly to the fact that the ZM-controlled fracture mechanism is topologically protected. The importance of notch-shape insensitivity lies in the fact that naturally occurring notches in materials take on diverse forms due to various types of damage. Achieving a metamaterial that guides cracks unidirectionally regardless of notch shape would greatly expand the applicability of fracture control in complex environments.

We demonstrate this through three representative cases (schematically depicted and color-coded in Fig. 5A): (I) a tilted cut in the bulk (green), (II) a cut at the soft edge (blue), and (III) a cut at the rigid edge (orange). For (I), we first check the distribution of ZMs predicted by theory for the idealized NN lattice under periodic boundary conditions (similar to Fig. 3A). After removing sites and bonds along the direction of lattice vector a_2 (Fig. 1B, Methods), all the ZMs are localized asymmetrically at only the right edge of the crack in Fig. 5D, as a result of topological polarization. We then examine the problem for the corresponding TMM in Fig. 5E. Simulations indicate that, under uniform stretching of the lattice, the deformation localizes at the right edge as well (see displacement colormap in Fig. 5E). Consequently, the stress developed in the hinges on the right edge is greater than that at the left edge, as depicted in Fig. 5B (left). A similar asymmetric pattern of ZMs and stress localization can also be found for other crack shapes (e.g., the triangular hole in Supplementary Fig. 19).

To quantify this asymmetry, we define n as the vector normal to the notch edge and α the angle between n and the polarization vector R_T. It is known from theory of polarized Maxwell lattices that the density of ZMs at an edge is proportional to n · R_T = cos α45. As described below, we find this quantity to be a good indicator of stress distribution around holes. In Fig. 5F, we consider holes of different orientations and plot the magnitude of ZMs at the edge and the bulk-to-edge stress ratio against the angle α. When α approaches π (or cos α → -1), the edge has no localized ZMs (the left side of the crack in Fig. 3A, Fig. 5D) and shows the same hinge stress as the bulk stress (Fig. 4A). On the other hand, as α goes to 0, the stress ratio approaches 0, implying a significant stress concentration at the edge. Here, the hinge thickness is set to h/|a_1| = 0.015 in Fig. 5B, C, F.

This asymmetry of stress distribution leads to robustly controllable crack propagation directions for a variety of hole orientations occurring in TMM domains, which we demonstrate numerically and experimentally in Fig. 5G, H. The initial state has a notch along a_2 in Fig. 5G. After being stretched, both nonlinear simulations and experiments show that the crack initially propagates to the right, emanating from the bottom-right tip and breaking sequentially the two adjacent hinges (Fig. 3G). After that, the crack also propagates to the left side, as shown in the Supplementary Movie 8, likely due to the proximity of the crack to the right boundary. The results emphasize that the unidirectional cracking mechanism is invariant to the shape of the bulk notch (see one-way cracking of a triangle notch in Supplementary Movie 9 and a rectangular notch in Supplementary Movie 10).

The same principle also controls stress fields and crack propagation driven by edge cuts, with some noteworthy differences between soft (cases II) and rigid (cases III) edges. In Fig. 5C, via simulations we calculate and plot the stress developed along the hinges in the same row along which the crack propagates, from the notch tip to the other side of the sample. We observe qualitatively different trends between the two cases. When the initial notch is at the soft edge, the stress drops sharply into the bulk, whereas when the initial notch is at the rigid edge, the stress decreases gradually. Overall, the decay of the soft edge curve follows a trend similar to the decay of hinge stress along the right tip path observed for the bulk crack in Fig. 4C. As shown in the experiment with initial notch at the soft edge (Fig. 5I–J), since the tip hinge has a much larger stress than the surrounding hinges (Fig. 5B, middle), the crack always propagates along the straight path (Fig. 5J). In contrast, the stress at the rigid edge is diffusive, uniformly distributed around the tip, as indicated by the color of the dots in the K inset (consistent with the numerical prediction in Fig. 5C). This results in multiple potential crack paths, as observed in the experiments documented in Fig. 5K–M. As a result, small random perturbations caused by experimental non-idealities can cause unexpected bifurcations of the cracking paths. In Fig. 5L, the crack turns directly into the direction along a_2. In the cases shown Fig. 5M, the crack propagates straightly first and then turns into the direction along a_2 at a later stage. Furthermore, in both simulations and experiments, the rigid edge exhibits delayed cracking compared to the soft edge (Supplementary Fig. 22E, F), despite similar force peaks in the force-displacement curves for cases (II) and (III).

These differences in fracturing behavior between the two edges suggest that crack tips in TMM display a variety of regimes, ranging from stable propagation at the soft tip to diffusive cracking at the rigid tip. Diffusive failures, characterized by fracturing without stress concentration, typically occur in systems with high disorder or low connectivity24,25,73. Previously, people achieve concentrated stress and diffusive stress tips in different systems by tuning network connectivity74 or rigidity9,24,25. The former appears in highly connected or rigid systems, while the latter shows up in systems with low connectivity. Here, we demonstrate that both concentrated and diffusive stress can emerge within the same over-constrained real system, allowing for on-demand fracturing control.

Programming fracture sequences and fracture resistance
Topologically controlled fracturing sequences can also be further programmed to control fracture resistance and mechanical stiffness in more versatile ways. By incorporating more polarization directions in the lattice, we can generate distinct cracking paths that result in tunable fracture resistance (Fig. 6). Here, we compare the single-domain TMM (with one polarization direction; see Fig. 1) to interface-TMMs (featuring two opposed polarization directions, Fig. 6A, C). In these systems, the programmed interfaces play a dominant role over the notch tips, due to the excited SSSs in the interfaces. In the photoelastic experiments, concentrated stress is clearly observed at the interfaces for both geometries (Fig. 6B, D), and this finding is consistent with the simulations. In Fig. 6E, F, cracks first originate in the interface regions (the gray box). Once the interface hinges fail, especially those in the zigzag interface near the notch and all hinges in the straight interface, the crack extends toward the notches. Owing to the topological polarization effect, the crack propagates to the right tip before reaching the left tip.

Furthermore, the shape of the interfaces influences not only the cracking path but also the force-displacement curves and fracture resistance (Fig. 6H). In the straight interface configuration, all interface units experience highly concentrated stress and break almost simultaneously (Fig. 6D, F–H), resulting in the earliest cracking and the most brittle behavior among the configurations. In contrast, the tortuous path in the zigzag interface geometry creates stress gradients, causing the interface units to break sequentially in a more gradual manner rather than all at once. As a result, the zigzag interface configuration absorbs more energy and exhibits the highest fracture toughness and linear elastic stiffness (Fig. 6H inset). These results highlight how topological features can be leveraged to precisely program stress distributions, crack sequences, and fracture resistance.
