## Methods

Experiments
We utilize Silhouette Cameo 4 Cutting Machine for cutting all the experiment samples. Our blade is the 0.2 mm Kraft Blade. We ensure that none of the hinges are broken before loading, to minimize initial imperfections. For the photoelastic setup in Fig. 1C and Supplementary Fig. 2, we set one polarizer in the front of the sample and the other behind the sample (with a 90 deg angle difference of the transmitting axis of the front one). The photo elastic thin film is PEI film with a thickness of 0.076 mm, purchased from McMASTER-CARR. The loading is performed quasi-statically, with a speed of 2 mm per minute. In Fig. 1, sample width w = 152.4 mm, sample length L = 157 mm, crack length 2a = 75 mm, and hinge thickness h ≈ 0.8 mm (h/|a_1| = 0.06) in Fig. 1H-L and Fig. 5G, H, I-M. Compared to idealized simulations, out-of-plane deformation in experimental tests of thin lattices can slow the rapid force drop and delays the cracking process77.

In Figs. 1 (D-M) and 5, the cardboard paper is the Wexford Folder 2-pocket (0.26 mm thick), purchased from Walgreens. Each paper sample weighs 3.6 g. The loading machine is Instron 4301 equipped with a 100 N loading cell and a 10 kN load cell. To allow uniform stretching/clamping at the top/bottom boundaries, we prepare four aluminum pieces (1.6 mm thick), sandwich each of the two sides between two pieces and glue them together. In Fig. 1D, for each of the three geometries, ten samples are loaded to observe the probabilities of fracturing direction.

In Fig. 2, we quantitatively characterize the triangular lattice, the regular kagome lattice, the twisted kagome lattice and the TMM. The ductility is measured as the elongation ratio at failure, Δ_c/l_0, where Δ_c is the critical displacement at the force peak and l_0 is the original sample length44. The fracture toughness is calculated as the critical stress intensity factor σ_c \sqrt{\pi a f(a/W)}, where σ_c is the critical stress applied, 2a is the full crack length, and f(a/W) is a specimen geometry dependent function of the crack length a and sample width W44. The consumed energy is ∫F dx, where F is the applied force and x is the displacement44. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 10H, fabricated hinge thickness shows a measure average 0.8 ± 0.2 mm. We measured 20% of the hinges in 10 representative samples (≈400 hinges in total). Notably, despite these minor fabrication errors, one-way cracking of the TMM is consistently observed across all specimens thanks to the topological protection, and error ranges of quantitative force-displacement curves remain within acceptable in Fig. 2B. The one-way propagation of cracks in the TMM is not affected by this variation, again demonstrating the robustness of topological mechanical effects.

In the material test, the strip samples have the size of 70 mm by 30 mm. Paper has two main axes (Figure)78, and in this work all the experimental stretching is along the length direction. In Supplementary Fig. 2D, the long edge of the strip is cut along the length direction of the paper folder.

The gripper rotated passively (side-notch results in Fig. 5) since it’s connected by a hinge. It mainly affects side cracks at the very end of the loading stage, due to the lack of constraints. For all the force-displacement measurements in this work, the cracks are in the bulk. The force-displacement curves measured in this work are all for bulk notches and therefore, the influence from top gripper rotation doesn’t affect the initial fracture events and plays a very minor role in the curves. For the sample in Supplementary Movie 2, after fracture initiates on the right, slight rotation of the grippers introduce mixed-mode loading conditions, leading to deviations in the crack path compared to idealized simulations. While this study focuses on the initial crack scenarios, the influence of boundary-induced mixed-mode effects is an important consideration for future work79.

Simulations
We use finite element software Abaqus/CAE 2023 for simulations80. Since we utilize cardboard paper as brittle material in experiments, we experimentally measured its stress-strain curve (Supplementary Fig. 2D, Supplementary Fig. 23A), and input that as the material parameters in the simulations. For spring-mass lattices, we apply truss elements (T2D3), which have no bending stiffness and can only carry axial stress. For continuous geometries, we choose reduced shell element (S4R).

We perform three types of simulations, linear frequency analysis (mode analysis in Figs. 3A, 5D), implicit static analysis (linear stress distribution in Figs. 1C, 3B, C, 4, and 5B, C, E, F) and explicit cracking simulations (Figs. 1 and 5H). For periodic boundary conditions (along x) in Figs. 3 and 5, we couple the degree of freedom of the left boundaries nodes with that of the right boundary nodes. The ZM weight is obtained via U_i = \sum ZM u_i^2, where i labels the nodes81. In explicit cracking simulations, we allow element deletion and strain failure criteria. For simplification and better visualization, the stress fields are normalized by comparing the stress to the largest stress in the system in Figs. 1A, H-L, 3C, 5. In all simulation results, the stress magnitude before normalization is between 0 and 7 × 10^7 Pa (Supplementary Fig. 23). In Fig. 1C, to compare the differences in stress distribution, we apply the displacement in the simulations, and then normalize the sum of extracted stresses in the three geometries to ensure that they exhibit the same total reaction stress.

For the implicit static analyses in Figs. 1C, 3G, 4 and 5B, C, F, we obtain a single value of stress out of a hinge with finite width. Since the stresses are concentrated at the hinges, we distribute extra fine meshes at all the hinges. For each hinge, we average the stresses over the elements at its thinnest cross-section (Supplementary Fig. 4).

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors investigated the fracture behaviors of topological mechanical metamaterials (TMMs) and compared their behavior with that of continuum material and regular Kagome lattices. They demonstrated the directional asymmetry in the fracture behavior of TMMs, which contrasts with the symmetry behaviors of continuum materials and regular Kagome lattices. Overall, the novelty of the current study is limited, as the authors primarily examined the fracture behaviors of an existing structure TMM, which has already been extensively studied (e.g., refs. [48-52]) including its fracture properties (ref. [56]). Furthermore, the current study lacks the depth, as it merely presents qualitative phenomena without providing a quantitative comparison of fracture toughness. The reported phenomena of directional asymmetry in fracture behavior are also not novel (PRL, 126, 025503, 2021). Furthermore, some claims appear to be overstated (see comment #4 below). Therefore, the current manuscript cannot be recommended for publication in Nature Communications. Specific comments are given below:
1. The novelty of the study is limited. There are many existing studies on TMMs, including those from the same authors (refs. [48-52, 56-60]). Regarding fracture properties, it is not surprising that such an asymmetric structure exhibits directional asymmetry in fracture behavior, as in one direction the crack tip is sharp and the structure is weaker while in the other direction the crack tip is blunt and the structure is stronger. The concept of “fracture unidirectionality feature” is not new either (ref. [39] PRL, 126, 025503, 2021). The current study simply demonstrates the directional asymmetry in fracture behavior for an existing structure without providing new insights into how such designs could achieve superior fracture resistance.
2. The current study does not provide any quantitative comparison beyond showing the phenomena. For example, in Fig. 1E and Fig. S6, only the normalized force (force/peak force) is reported. The authors are suggested to provide the absolute force-displacement curves and calculate the fracture toughness of TMMs, and compare these results with those of regular Kagome lattices and other benchmark lattices, such as triangular lattices. Because it would be better to confirm whether TMMs achieve such fracture properties at significant expense of load-bearing capacity.
3. Even though using the normalized force, it seems that the regular Kagome lattices experimentally outperforms the TMMs in terms of fracture resistance (Fig. S6C). Furthermore, the discrepancy between simulations and experiments should be addressed.
4. In the Introduction Line 26, the claim of “Despite this abundance of approaches, a robust general principle for using geometry to guide the direction of fractures is still lacking.” seems overstated. The current study does not seem to provide a robust general principle either. In Line 50, it is stated that “the TMM is light-weighted and features material-invariant and scale-invariant properties.” Although it may be true for “material-invariant and scale-invariant”, there are no results in the manuscript that directly support this.
5. In Fig. 4, it is seen that the upper gripper rotated during loading. The authors are suggested to improve the mechanical testing setup to ensure uniaxial loading and provide the loading-displacement curves to make the results more quantitative. Moreover, the demonstration in Fig. 4 is too simple. It would be better to show how to engineer a tortuous crack path that leads to superior toughness through such asymmetry design.

### Reviewer 2

The paper by Wang et al. uses topological metamaterials to control fracture. In particular, since topological metamaterials are polarized---they host asymmetric floppy modes, the fracture propagation becomes unidirectional and leads to large deformations before failure. As a consequence, the metamaterial appears ductile even though it is made from a brittle material.
As clearly described in the manuscript, the mechanism at stake is stress asymmetry, that comes from the topological polarization, the distorted Kagome unit cells are floppy on one side, therefore tend to deform without stretching any of the bonds on this side. In contrast, the opposite size exhibits no such zero energy deformation and the bonds tend to stretch when load is applied. What the authors show is that this simplified picture of the balls-and-springs holds even when the metamaterial is made from a continuous material rather than discrete springs, i.e. when the geometry is made from real hinges. Whereas the floppy hinges exhibit low stress, the opposite hinges undergo high stresses and hence break first. This is the reason why the fractures tends to propagate in one direction and, as the authors show, even turn around when the notch is created on the side with high stresses.
The main take away from this work is that topological metamaterials offer a new paradigm to control fracture, in a way that is very different from classical fracture mechanics. Fracture metamaterials have recently emerged as a promising area of research, but so far broadly applicable design concepts are missing. The present work establishes topology as a promising approach and hold the potential to become a seminal work. Therefore I think this paper is potentially an excellent fit for Nature Communications. I however think that the control of fracture displayed in the manuscript in its present form remains rather limited. The key attribute of metamaterials is their tunability. I think that the manuscript would reach a much higher impact if the authors were able to provide more compelling demonstrations of fracture control by utilizing further the design freedom at their disposal and topological floppy modes as a guide. Besides this main concern (which I believe the authors are well equipped to address), I list below some comments, which might help the authors further improve their manuscript.
*1 The authors argue that the unidirectionality of the fracture is protected by topology and is therefore less sensitive to defects and imperfection. It would perhaps be worth to back up that statement, especially since fracture is a phenomenon that is known to be extremely sensitive to imperfections. In particular, to which extend is the approach more robust that the asymmetric fracture reported in ref [39]?
*2 Is topology really essential here? What happens if one take a twisted (undistorted) Kagome instead? Would such metamaterial exhibit symmetric fracture instead?
*3 Likewise, does the magnitude of the topological polarization matter for unidirectional facture propagation? I would expect a topological metamaterials with a small polarization/asymmetry to be less robust to imperfections?
*4 Section 2.2 can be understood by physicists well versed in topological metamaterials but less so by scientists with no background in this area. The authors might want to make that section a bit more pedagogical to extend the reach of their paper.
*5 The authors often refer to supplementary figures from the Main Text, which make the read somewhat cumbersome and gives the impression that key information is given in the SI rather than in the Main Text. For instance, the comparison with continuous media in Fig. 1 is somewhat of a naive benchmark. From the text it seems that comparing with the undistorted Kagome would be more meaningful (and would allow less back and forth between Main Text and Supplementary Information).
*6 Topological metamaterials can host states of self-stress. What is the role of those states of self stress on the fracture propagation?
*7 Higher order topological metamaterials can host corner modes, would such corner modes be beneficial for the control of fracture?
*8 More generally, to reflect my main concern above, it would be important to know what the range of control one can achieve with topological metamaterials as well at the limitations.
